about: Written by scripts/build-explorer-index.mjs from client/public/explorer/stops, threads.json, cards.json, films.json and films/. Do not edit by hand.

summary.younger: God made everything out of nothing, and he made people to know him and to take care of his world.
summary.older: Before anything else, there is God. He speaks the world into being, calls it good, and makes people in his image to care for it under him.

summary.younger: The first people did not trust God and did what he told them not to do. Sin and sadness came into the world, but God kept caring for them.
summary.older: Adam and Eve reach for what God withheld, and the damage spreads: shame, blame, murder, the flood, a tower built to reach the sky. God judges, and he keeps showing mercy.

summary.younger: God chose Abraham and promised him a family as many as the stars, a land to live in, and a blessing for the whole world.
summary.older: God answers a scattered world by calling one man and making him a promise: a people, a land, and a blessing that will reach every family on earth.

summary.younger: God's people were slaves in Egypt. God set them free on the night of the Passover and led them through the sea.
summary.older: Abraham's family has become a nation of slaves. God hears them, sends Moses, spares them by the blood of a lamb, and opens a road through the sea.

summary.younger: At a mountain called Sinai, God gave his people his good laws and told them to build a tent where he would live among them.
summary.older: Rescued people are given a way to live. At Sinai God makes a covenant with Israel, gives the law, and has them build the tabernacle so that he can dwell among them.

summary.younger: God brought his people into the land he had promised. They kept forgetting him, and God kept sending leaders to rescue them.
summary.older: God keeps his word and gives the land. Then a cycle begins: the people turn away, trouble comes, they cry out, God sends a judge. Each time round it gets worse.

stops.title: The Kingdom
stops.range: 1 Samuel to 1 Kings 11, and the Psalms

summary.younger: God gave Israel kings. The greatest was David, a shepherd boy, and God promised that a king from his family would rule for ever.
summary.older: Israel asks for a king. Saul fails; David loves God and fails badly too; God promises him a son whose kingdom will never end. Solomon builds the temple.

stops.title: The Prophets and Exile
stops.range: 1 Kings 12 to 2 Kings 25, and the Prophets

summary.younger: The people stopped listening to God. Prophets warned them, but they would not turn back, and they were taken far from home.
summary.older: The kingdom splits, its kings lead the people to idols, and God sends prophets to call them back. They will not come. Assyria takes the north and Babylon burns Jerusalem, yet the prophets promise a new covenant and a coming king.

summary.younger: God brought some of his people home. They rebuilt the temple and the city walls, and then they waited a long time for God's promised king.
summary.older: Some exiles come home under Persian rule and rebuild the temple and the walls, but no son of David sits on the throne. The Old Testament ends looking ahead, and roughly four centuries pass before the next page.

summary.younger: God the Son was born as a baby named Jesus. He healed people, taught about God's kingdom, and showed what God is like.
summary.older: God keeps his promises in person. Jesus, born of Mary, announces that God's kingdom has come near, heals and forgives, calls twelve disciples, and speaks with an authority that belongs to God alone.

stops.title: The Cross and the Empty Tomb

summary.younger: Jesus died on a cross to take away the sin of the world. On the third day God raised him from the dead. He is alive.
summary.older: Jesus dies on a Roman cross at Passover, carrying the sin of the world, and on the third day God raises him bodily from the dead.

summary.younger: Jesus went back to his Father and sent the Holy Spirit. His followers told the good news about Jesus to people everywhere.
summary.older: Fifty days after Passover the Spirit comes. The church begins in Jerusalem and spreads, Jews and Gentiles together, until the news of Jesus reaches Rome.

stops.title: The New Creation
stops.range: Revelation 21 to 22, with 1 Corinthians 15 and Romans 8

summary.younger: One day Jesus will come back and make everything new. God will live with his people, and there will be no more crying or pain.
summary.older: The story ends where it began, with God and his people together, in a garden that has become a city. Jesus returns, death is undone, and God makes his home with people for ever.

line.younger: From the first page to the last, God wants to live with his people. Follow the places where he makes his home.
line.older: The whole Bible can be read as one long answer to a question: can God live with his people? Watch where he dwells move from a garden to a tent, a temple, a person, a people, and a whole new world.

key.apart: The closeness is lost, or still waited for

creation.line: God planted a garden and put the people he made there, close to him.

fall.line: The man and the woman hid from God among the trees, and they were sent out of the garden.

abraham.line: God came to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Jacob woke from a dream and said the LORD was in that place.

rescue.line: God went ahead of his people in a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night.

sinai.line: God told Israel to build a tent, the tabernacle, so that he could dwell among them, and his glory filled it.

land.line: In the land, the tent of meeting was set up at Shiloh, among the tribes.

kingdom.line: Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem, and the cloud of God's glory filled it.

exile.line: The prophet Ezekiel saw God's glory leave the temple before Babylon destroyed it.

return.line: The people rebuilt the temple, and God promised that one day he would fill it with glory.

jesus.line: Jesus is God with us. The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us.

cross.line: When Jesus died, the curtain that closed off the most holy place in the temple tore from top to bottom.

church.line: God's Spirit came to live in his people. Paul tells the church that it is now God's temple.

new-creation.line: At the end, God's dwelling place is with people, and he lives with them for ever.

line.younger: God makes promises to his people, and he always keeps them.
line.older: God binds himself to people by covenant: with Noah, Abraham, Israel at Sinai and David, and at last the new covenant in Jesus.

key.made: God makes a covenant promise, or renews it

fall.line: After the flood God set his rainbow in the clouds as “a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth.”

abraham.line: The LORD made a covenant with Abram, and promised that “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you.”

rescue.line: God heard his people groaning in Egypt, “and He remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.”

sinai.line: At Sinai God said, “if you will indeed obey My voice and keep My covenant, you will be My treasured possession.”

land.line: In the land, “Not one of all the LORD’s good promises to the house of Israel had failed; everything was fulfilled.”

kingdom.line: God promised David a son whose throne would last for ever. A psalm sings, “I have made a covenant with My chosen one.”

exile.line: The people had broken the covenant, and God promised a new one: “I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts.”

return.line: The people came home and waited. Malachi promised that the Lord they were seeking would come to his temple: “the Messenger of the covenant, in whom you delight.”

jesus.line: Before Jesus was born, Zechariah sang that God had come to remember “His holy covenant, the oath He swore to our father Abraham.”

cross.line: At the last supper Jesus took the cup and said, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you.”

church.line: Paul writes that every one of God's promises is “Yes” in Christ.

new-creation.line: At the end the old promise is kept in full: “They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God.”

line.younger: Again and again in the Bible, an animal is given in someone's place, or a lamb is a sign of rescue, until Jesus, the Lamb of God.
line.older: Sacrifice runs from the garden to the cross: a covering, a substitute, a lamb that marks a rescued home, a goat that carries wrongs away, until the one sacrifice of Jesus, the Lamb of God.

key.points: A sacrifice points ahead: a covering, a substitute, a lamb
key.lamb: Jesus, the Lamb of God, and his one sacrifice

fall.line: After they sinned, God himself made garments of skin and clothed the man and the woman: a better covering than the leaves they had sewn.

abraham.line: On the mountain Abraham told Isaac, “God Himself will provide the lamb,” and God provided a ram, offered “in place of his son.”

rescue.line: At the first Passover each family's lamb marked their home. God said, “when I see the blood, I will pass over you.”

sinai.line: On the Day of Atonement the high priest laid the people's wrongs on a goat, which carried them away into the wilderness.

land.line: In the land, camped at Gilgal, the people kept the Passover, remembering the lamb and the rescue.

kingdom.line: David learned that God wants more than offerings: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit.”

exile.line: Isaiah spoke of a servant who “was led like a lamb to the slaughter.” Christians, from the first church on, read that servant as Jesus; many Jewish readers read him as the people of Israel.

return.line: When the temple was rebuilt, the exiles who had come home kept the Passover again.

jesus.line: John the Baptist saw Jesus coming and said, “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!”

cross.line: Jesus died at Passover, when the Passover lamb was sacrificed. Paul writes, “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.”

church.line: The letter to the Hebrews says Jesus “offered for all time one sacrifice for sins” and sat down at God's right hand.

new-creation.line: In the city there is no need of sun or moon: “the glory of God illuminates the city, and the Lamb is its lamp.”

line.younger: God's people wait for a good king, and Jesus is that king.
line.older: People made to rule under God want to rule without him. The story looks for the true king, the son of David, who reigns by serving.

key.reigns: God's rule is shown, or his king is on the throne
key.waited: The king is promised, or the throne stands empty

creation.line: God made people in his image to rule over his world under him, caring for it as he would.

fall.line: People grabbed at ruling without God. Then God promised that the woman's seed would crush the serpent's head.

abraham.line: God promised Abraham, “kings will descend from you.”

rescue.line: At the sea God showed who really rules, and Moses and Israel sang, “The LORD will reign forever and ever!”

sinai.line: At Sinai, God, Israel's true king, made his people “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.”

land.line: Judges ends sadly: “In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes.”

kingdom.line: God promised David a son whose kingdom would last: “your throne will be established forever.”

exile.line: When Babylon took Jerusalem, David's throne was lost. Isaiah had promised a child who “will reign on the throne of David.”

return.line: The people came home, but no son of David sat on the throne. Zechariah told them, “See, your King comes to you.”

jesus.line: Jesus announced that “the kingdom of God is near,” and Peter said he was the Christ, the promised king.

cross.line: The soldiers crowned Jesus with thorns, and the charge over the cross read “THE KING OF THE JEWS.” On the third day God raised him.

church.line: God seated the risen Jesus at his right hand and made him “head over everything for the church,” which is his body.

new-creation.line: At the end, “The throne of God and of the Lamb will be within the city,” and his people reign with him for ever.

line.younger: God's Holy Spirit is at work from the first page to the last: making, giving life, helping people God chose for a task, and at last living in all God's people.
line.older: The Spirit of God hovers over the first waters, comes on judges, kings and prophets for a task, is promised for all God's people, rests on Jesus, and is poured out at Pentecost to live in the church.

key.works: The Spirit is at work: making, giving life, or coming on someone for a task
key.promised: The Spirit is promised for all God's people, and waited for
key.poured: The Spirit is poured out and lives in God's people

creation.line: At the very beginning, “the Spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters.”

abraham.line: Even Pharaoh saw God at work in Joseph, and asked, “Can we find anyone like this man, in whom the Spirit of God abides?”

rescue.line: Long afterward, Isaiah looked back on the crossing of the sea and spoke of God as the One “who set His Holy Spirit among them.”

sinai.line: God filled Bezalel “with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge” to make the tent where God would live among his people.

land.line: The Spirit of the LORD came upon Gideon and other judges for a task. Moses had wished that the LORD would put his Spirit on all his people.

kingdom.line: When Samuel anointed David, “the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward.” Later David prayed, “take not Your Holy Spirit from me.”

exile.line: In the exile God promised a new heart: “I will put My Spirit within you.” Joel heard God promise to pour out his Spirit on all people.

return.line: To the people rebuilding the temple God said, “My Spirit remains among you; do not be afraid,” and the work would be done “Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit.”

jesus.line: At his baptism Jesus saw “the Spirit descending on Him like a dove,” and he said, “The Spirit of the Lord is on Me.”

cross.line: The night before he died, Jesus promised his friends another Advocate, the Spirit of truth. Risen, he told them to wait in the city until they were “clothed with power from on high.”

church.line: At Pentecost “they were all filled with the Holy Spirit.” Paul tells the church that God's Spirit dwells in them: they are God's temple.

new-creation.line: On the Bible's last page the Spirit and the bride, the church, both say “Come,” inviting everyone who is thirsty to the water of life.

line.younger: God's plan was always for people from every country.
line.older: Through Abraham's family God means to bless all the families of the earth, and the last pages show people from every nation together.

key.reaches: God's blessing reaches people of many nations
key.promised: The blessing for every nation is promised, or still waited for

creation.line: God blessed the first people and told them to “fill the earth.” Paul says that from one man God made every nation.

fall.line: At Babel people built a tower to “make a name for ourselves,” and the LORD scattered them over the face of all the earth.

abraham.line: God chose one family for the sake of every family: “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you.”

rescue.line: When Israel left Egypt, “a mixed multitude also went up with them.” From the start, others went with God's people.

sinai.line: God's law told Israel to love the foreigner living among them “as yourself, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.”

land.line: Rahab of Jericho and Ruth from Moab joined God's people. Ruth told Naomi, “your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.”

kingdom.line: At the temple Solomon prayed for the foreigner who comes from a distant land: “Then all the peoples of the earth will know Your name.”

exile.line: God sent Jonah to Nineveh because he cared about “the great city of Nineveh.” Isaiah heard God promise a servant who would be “a light for the nations.”

return.line: After the return, Malachi heard God say, “My name will be great among the nations, from where the sun rises to where it sets.”

jesus.line: Magi from the east came to worship the child Jesus, and old Simeon called him “a light for revelation to the Gentiles.”

cross.line: The risen Jesus sent his friends to “make disciples of all nations.”

church.line: At Pentecost people from many lands heard “the wonders of God” in their own languages, and Peter learned that God “welcomes those from every nation who fear Him.”

new-creation.line: John saw “a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue,” before the throne, and the leaves of the tree of life are “for the healing of the nations.”

cards.title: God
cards.pictureLabel: The river Jordan between low hills: a figure stands in the water, a dove comes down through an opening in the sky, and light falls from beyond the top of the picture.

statement.younger: There is one God. He made everything, he never began and he will never end, and nothing made him. The Bible shows him to us as the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit: one God, not three.
statement.older: There is one true and living God: Spirit, without beginning or end, the maker of everything that is. The Bible speaks of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit each as God, and keeps the three distinct, yet there is one God. The church says it this way: one in being and three in persons, each fully God, and one God. The family catechism calls it ‘not a riddle to solve but a wonder to receive’.

quote.text: baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit

question.ask: How could anyone know that God is really there?
question.younger: No one can prove it the way you prove a sum, and some careful thinkers do not believe it. But Christians give reasons. Everything we know came from something, and the whole universe could have been different, or not been at all. So why is there anything? Christians believe the answer is God, who is not one more thing needing a maker. And they believe God has shown himself most fully in Jesus.
question.older: LiveWell's Honest Answer does not claim a proof in the mathematician's sense. It weighs reasons, each open to inspection: that anything exists at all, when the universe could have been different or not been at all; that the universe is fit for life; and that some things are really wrong. It gives the case against at its strongest, including Bertrand Russell's reply that the universe is ‘just there, and that's all’, and it says plainly that this is the step where an honest person can disagree. Even if the reasons succeed, they do not yet show that God is three persons or that he became a man; for Christians that rests on whether Jesus was raised. A person can weigh all of it and still say no. What nobody can honestly say is that there is nothing to weigh.

deeper.label: Does God actually exist?
How can God be three and one?
The family catechism: is God one, or is God three?

cards.title: The Bible
cards.pictureLabel: An open Bible on a table under an arched window.

statement.younger: The Bible is God's true Word. God gave it through many writers over a very long time, and it tells one big story, about Jesus saving us.
statement.older: The Bible is sixty-six books written by many people over many centuries, and through those human writers God himself speaks. It is God-breathed, true in all it teaches, and Jesus is its center: he said the Scriptures testify about him.

quote.text: All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work.

question.ask: How can a book written by people be God's Word?
question.younger: God used real people, with their own words and their own ways of writing. The Holy Spirit carried them along, so that what they wrote is what God wanted to say.
question.older: Christians do not say the writers took dictation. Luke says he carefully investigated everything before he wrote (Luke 1:3). They say God was at work in the whole of it, so that men “spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21). That is a claim to weigh, not to swallow, and the questions about how the books were copied and collected are fair ones.

deeper.label: Why would anyone trust the Bible?
The family catechism: how has God spoken to us?

cards.title: People made in God's image
cards.pictureLabel: A man and a woman in a garden at morning: one plants a young tree, the other carries a jar of water, and a still pool between them gives back the light.

statement.younger: God made people, boys and girls, in his own image. That means every person was made to know God, to show what he is like, and to take care of his world. It is God's gift, so every person matters, whatever they can or cannot do.
statement.older: In the ancient world a king could be called the image of a god. Genesis gives that dignity to every human being, male and female. The family catechism says it means we were made to know God, to reflect his character, and to rule over and care for his world as those who answer to him. The image is given, not earned, so it does not rise and fall with what a person can do.

quote.text: So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them.

question.ask: Why should every person be worth the same, when people are so different?
question.younger: People are good at different things, and some cannot do much at all, like a tiny baby or someone who is very ill. If being worth something depended on what you can do, some people would be worth less. Christians believe every person's worth is given by God, who made them in his image, so nobody can earn it and nobody can lose it. Many people who do not believe in God also believe every person matters, and they live it well.
question.older: LiveWell's Honest Answer starts from something nearly everyone already believes: a newborn, a man with advanced dementia and the most gifted adult in the room have equal worth. Abilities come in degrees and can be lost, so a worth that rested on them would come in degrees and could be lost. A worth that is given by God, not earned, is equal and can't be lost. The answer says plainly that this is an argument about what best explains a belief most people share, not a proof; that people who don't believe in God hold the same belief sincerely and live it well; and that it doesn't show that anyone who rejects God values people less.

deeper.label: What makes us human in the age of AI?
How should a Christian read Genesis 1?
The family catechism: what does it mean to be made in God's image?

cards.title: Sin
cards.pictureLabel: A garden in the evening breeze: two people hide among the bushes, thorns grow at the edge of the path, and a light comes along the path toward them.

statement.younger: Sin is when we do not love God and other people the way we should: doing what God says not to do, or not doing what he says to do. Everyone has sinned. Sin breaks things between us and God, and between people. But God comes looking for us, and he sent Jesus to bring us home.
statement.older: The family catechism calls sin any failure to love God and others as we should, whether by doing what God forbids or by failing to do what he commands. At its root it is not trusting that God is good, and putting ourselves in his place. Everyone has sinned, and the damage runs every way: with God, with each other, inside ourselves, and with the world. Yet in the same chapter that tells of the first sin, God comes looking and calls, “Where are you?”

quote.text: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.

question.ask: Does God stop loving people when they do wrong?
question.younger: No. God does not wait for people to be good before he loves them. The Bible says that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Jesus told a story about a son who ran away and wasted everything. When he came home, his father ran to meet him and hugged him. When we do wrong, we can tell God we are sorry, and he forgives us because of Jesus.
question.older: The family catechism answers no: God's love for his children does not rise when they are good or fall when they are bad, because it was never based on them in the first place. It came first: “While we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). In Jesus' story of the lost son, the father sees him while he is “still in the distance”, is “filled with compassion”, and runs (Luke 15:20). Sin is serious, and it grieves God; that is why the cross was needed. But the way home stays open: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9).

deeper.label: Sin: what the Bible teaches, and where Christians differ
The family catechism: what is sin?
The family catechism: will God ever stop loving me if I am bad?

cards.title: Jesus, God and man
cards.pictureLabel: A manger full of straw in a stable at night, under one bright star.

statement.younger: Jesus is God the Son. He became a real man, born as a baby, so that he could save us. He is fully God and fully man.
statement.older: Jesus is one person who is truly God and truly man; the church confessed it in those words at the Council of Chalcedon in 451. He was with God and was God from the beginning, and he became flesh: he grew tired, he wept, he died. Only someone who is both could bring God and people back together.

quote.text: The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.

question.ask: If Jesus is God, who was he praying to?
question.younger: He was praying to God the Father. There is one God, who is the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Son loves to talk with the Father.
question.older: To God the Father. Christians confess one God in three persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Jesus praying shows that the Son and the Father are two persons, not that Jesus is less than God. The same Gospel that shows him praying ends with Thomas calling him “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28).

deeper.label: Was Jesus just a good teacher?
How can God be three and one?
The family catechism: who is Jesus Christ?

cards.title: The cross
cards.pictureLabel: An empty cross on a hill at first light, with a path from the foot of the picture leading up to it and the sun rising behind the far hills.

statement.younger: Jesus never did anything wrong, but he died on a cross for our sins. Nobody forced him: the Father sent the Son because he loves us, and the Son gave his life freely. At the cross God mended what sin broke, and on the third day Jesus rose again.
statement.older: Christians confess that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that the cross is God's own act of love: the Father sent the Son, and the Son laid down his life of his own accord. It is not an angry Father against an unwilling Son. The Bible uses many pictures for what the cross did: the Passover lamb, a ransom, our sins borne in our place, victory over sin, death and the devil, love shown, and enemies made friends. Christians hold them together, and some traditions put one at the centre. The creed does not choose a theory; it says he came ‘for us men and for our salvation’.

quote.text: For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God.

question.younger: Some of the leaders in Jerusalem wanted to get rid of Jesus. One of his own friends, Judas, helped them arrest him at night. They handed him over to Pilate, the Roman governor, and Pilate had him put to death on a cross. Jesus and his first friends were Jewish, and it is wrong to blame the Jewish people for his death. The Bible says he died for the sins of every one of us, and that he gave his life freely.
question.older: The Gospels answer with care. The chief priests and their council handed him over; Pilate, the Roman governor, condemned him; Roman soldiers crucified him. Jesus himself, his disciples and the first church were Jews, and blaming the Jewish people for his death is a lie that Christians must reject plainly. The New Testament places all people inside the guilt: Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and the people of Israel together (Acts 4:27), and in the end every one of us, because “Christ died for our sins” (1 Corinthians 15:3). And Jesus said of his life, “No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord” (John 10:18).

deeper.label: Ways of explaining the cross: the Study Bible's note on Romans 3
The family catechism: why did Jesus have to die?
Did the resurrection actually happen?

cards.title: The resurrection
cards.pictureLabel: A tomb cut in the rock of a garden at first light, its round stone rolled aside and its doorway open and empty; on a far hill, an empty cross.

statement.younger: Jesus did not stay dead. On the third day God raised him from the grave, in his body, and he is alive. Because he lives, death is not the end for those who belong to him.
statement.older: Christians confess that on the third day Jesus rose bodily from the grave: an event, not a picture or a nice idea about spring. The whole faith stands on it; Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, faith is futile. And Christ is the firstfruits: his rising is the start of the resurrection promised to all who belong to him.

quote.text: But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.

question.ask: How could anyone know that Jesus really rose?
question.younger: No one can prove it the way you prove a sum. But there are things almost every historian agrees on: Jesus really died; very soon his followers were sure they had seen him alive; two people who did not believe, Paul and Jesus' brother James, came to believe; and his friends began telling people in Jerusalem, where he was buried. Other explanations each fit part of this and struggle with the rest. Christians believe God raised him.
question.older: History can't prove a miracle, and LiveWell's Honest Answer does not pretend it can. It starts from a short list of facts that nearly every historian of the period accepts, skeptics included: Jesus was crucified, his followers were soon convinced they had seen him alive, a persecutor and a doubting brother came to believe the same, and the preaching began in the city where he was buried. Each natural explanation covers part of the evidence and strains at the rest. Whether a person can accept the one that covers all of it depends on whether they have already decided that God can't act. You can weigh it all and still say no; even among the eleven, when they saw him, some doubted (Matthew 28:17).

deeper.label: Did the resurrection actually happen?
Does God actually exist? (the question this one turns on)
The family catechism: did Jesus stay dead?

cards.title: The Holy Spirit
cards.pictureLabel: A hillside in the wind: the grass and a tree bend the same way and a breath line sweeps across the sky; three people walk up a path together, and one small flame burns in the sky above them.

statement.younger: The Holy Spirit is God, the third person of the Trinity, not a force or a feeling. You cannot see him, as you cannot see the wind, but you can see what he does. He gives new life to people who trust Jesus, lives in every one of them, helps them pray, and slowly makes them more like Jesus.
statement.older: Christians confess the Holy Spirit as fully God, the third person of the Trinity, the one the Nicene Creed calls ‘the Lord and Giver of Life’, ‘who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified’. He gives new birth, joins believers to Christ, lives in every one of them, grows his fruit in them and gives gifts for the good of the whole church. All Christians confess this. Churches differ on whether some gifts, such as speaking in tongues, prophecy and healing, continue as they did in Acts, and on when and how a believer receives the Spirit; this card does not choose between them.

quote.text: The wind blows where it wishes. You hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it is going. So it is with everyone born of the Spirit.

question.ask: Is the Holy Spirit a person, or a power?
question.younger: A person. The Bible says people can lie to the Holy Spirit and make him sad, and you can only do that to a person. When a man lied to the Holy Spirit, Peter told him he had lied to God. The Holy Spirit is not a part of God or a feeling: he is God, with the Father and the Son.
question.older: A person, and God. LiveWell's Honest Answer on the Trinity points to Peter, who told a man who had chosen “to lie to the Holy Spirit” that “You have not lied to men, but to God” (Acts 5:3-4). Paul writes, “do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Ephesians 4:30), and a power cannot be grieved. The creeds say each person is wholly God, not a third of God, and the answer adds that the Father, the Son and the Spirit never act apart. It also says plainly what remains a mystery: how one God is three persons is something no one can see to the bottom of, which is not the same as a contradiction.

deeper.label: How can God be three and one?
Where churches differ on the gifts: the Study Bible's notes on Acts 2
The family catechism: who is the Holy Spirit?

cards.title: The church
cards.pictureLabel: People of different kinds seated together round one table, with an open book, bread and a cup on it, under one roof and one lamp.

statement.younger: The church is God's family who follow Jesus together. It is not first a building. It is people, gathered by God's Spirit around Jesus, to worship God, to love one another and to tell others about him.
statement.older: The church is the whole company of God's people, gathered by the Spirit around Christ, called to worship God, love one another, and make him known to the world; that is how the family catechism words it. Paul calls it one body with many parts, and Peter a house of living stones. God saves people into a family, not alone.

quote.text: They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer.

question.ask: If there is one church, why do churches do things so differently?
question.younger: Churches do some things differently, like how they baptize and how they are led. But all who trust Jesus belong to his one church, with one Lord. Faithful Christians differ on these things and still call one another brothers and sisters.
question.older: Churches share the confession of one Lord, the command Jesus gave to baptize in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the meal he gave, which proclaims “the Lord’s death until He comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26). They differ on who should be baptized (those old enough to confess faith, or also the children of believers) and how (by going under the water, or by pouring or sprinkling it), on what happens in the Lord's Supper, and on how churches are led (by bishops, by elders, or by the congregation deciding together). Faithful churches differ on these while confessing one Lord, and this card does not choose between them. The Study Bible's notes on Acts 2 and 1 Corinthians 11 set out each view.

deeper.label: Baptism: the Study Bible's notes on Acts 2
The Lord's Supper: the Study Bible's notes on 1 Corinthians 11
Can you be a Christian without going to church?
The family catechism: what is the church?

cards.title: The life to come
cards.pictureLabel: A seed sown in the dark soil, shown in a cut through the ground, its root going down and its stalk rising into a full ear of wheat; far off, a city wall with its gate standing open and light coming from it.

statement.younger: Death is real and sad, but for those who belong to Jesus it is not the end. They go to be with him. One day Jesus will come back, raise their bodies new and whole, and make everything new, and God will wipe away every tear.
statement.older: Christians confess, in the words of the Apostles' Creed, ‘the resurrection of the body; and the life everlasting’. Jesus will return in glory to judge the living and the dead and to make all things new. The final hope is not a soul escaping the body but the body raised, as Christ's was: he is the firstfruits, and Paul compares the body to a seed that is sown and comes up new. Christians confess a real judgment, and they differ on how to understand what it will be like; the site's Honest Answer on hell adds, ‘Whatever hell is, it isn't what God wants for anyone.’ They also read the order and timing of the last events differently; all confess that Christ will come again, and no one knows the day or the hour.

quote.text: ‘He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,’ and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the former things have passed away.

question.younger: Their body stops, and that is real and sad; when his friend Lazarus died, Jesus cried. But the person does not stop being. The Bible says that people who trust Jesus go to be with him, and wait for the day he raises their bodies new. Christians do not all describe that waiting the same way, but they all hope for the same day. If someone you love has died, it helps to talk about it with a parent or another grown-up you trust.
question.older: Death is real, and the Bible never pretends otherwise. Christians confess that the dead in Christ will be raised bodily when he returns. On the time between, the Study Bible's notes set out two readings. Most Christian traditions read Jesus' words to the dying man, “Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43), with Paul's wish to be “away from the body and at home with the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:8), as a promise of being with Christ, awake and known, straight after death. Others place the comma after ‘today’ and hold that the dead sleep until the resurrection. Christians still differ on how to describe that time; the hope they share is the resurrection of the body. If a death has hit you hard, talk with a parent, a pastor or a leader you trust.

films.title: The Holy Spirit through the Bible

line.older: From the waters of Genesis 1 to the last invitation of Revelation 22, in eight pictures. The Holy Spirit is God, a person, not a force.

line.older: One light, followed from a garden to a tent, a temple, a person, a people and a whole new world: the Bible's long answer to whether God can live with his people.

line.younger: God's people waited a long time for a good king. Seven pictures follow one crown, from a shepherd boy to a cross to a throne that lasts for ever.
line.older: The king through the whole Bible in seven pictures: God's rule, the shepherd king, the promise to David, the empty throne, the son of David, the King on a cross, and the kingdom.

line.younger: God makes promises and keeps them. Seven pictures follow the covenants, from Noah's rainbow to the cup Jesus shared, each one laid on the one before like the stones of an arch.
line.older: The covenants through the whole Bible in seven pictures: Noah, Abraham, Sinai, David, the new covenant promised, the cup at the supper, and every promise kept in Christ.

line.younger: From the garden to the last page, God provides. Seven pictures follow a covering, a ram, the Passover lamb and the altar to Jesus, the Lamb of God, and the Lamb at the center of the throne.
line.older: Sacrifice through the whole Bible in seven pictures: a covering, the ram in Isaac's place, the Passover, the Day of Atonement, the Lamb of God, one sacrifice for all time, and the Lamb on the throne.

line.younger: The Bible talks about blood from its first pages to the cross. Seven pictures show why: blood means a life given, and God himself gives it.
line.older: Why does the Bible speak so much of blood? Seven pictures follow its own answer from the first altars to the cross: a life given in place of another, and God the one who gives it.

line.younger: Again and again in the Bible, God's people are far from home, and again and again God brings them back. Seven pictures follow one road, from the garden gate to a city whose gates are never shut.
line.older: Exile and homecoming through the whole Bible in seven pictures: the garden, Egypt, Babylon, the return, Jesus, believers as foreigners on the way, and the city at the end.

line.younger: God chose one family so that every family on earth could be blessed. Follow that promise from a tower left unfinished to a crowd no one can count.
line.older: From Babel's scattering to the multitude before the throne: how the promise to Abraham, a blessing for all the families of the earth, runs through the whole Bible.

line.younger: Jesus said the kingdom of God is like a tiny seed that grows into a great tree. Seven pictures watch it grow, from God's rule over all to the day it comes in full.
line.older: The kingdom of God in seven pictures: God's rule over all, the kingdom come near in Jesus, its signs, the mustard seed, the order turned upside down, a kingdom not of this world, and already and not yet.

line.younger: The Bible begins in the dark and ends in a city with no night. Follow one light all the way through.
line.older: From “Let there be light” to the city that needs no sun: the Bible's light followed through Egypt, the wilderness, the tent, Isaiah's promise and the words of Jesus.

line.older: One God in three persons: what the Bible shows, why the usual pictures break, and why the church kept the Bible's words instead. In eight pictures.

line.older: Creation out of nothing, a world called very good, and people made in God's image: what that means, why it is a gift, and what Christians leave open. In seven pictures.

line.younger: What sin is, what it breaks, and what God does about it, in six pictures.
line.older: Sin at its root, the four things it breaks, why it touches everyone, and the God who comes looking. In six pictures.

line.older: The Word with God from the beginning, born as a man, fully God and fully man in one person, and the question he asked his friends. In seven pictures.

line.younger: What happened on the cross, and the Bible's own pictures of what it did for us, in eight pictures.
line.older: What happened at the cross, and six pictures the Bible itself uses for what it did, held together, in eight moving pictures.

line.older: What the resurrection is and what it means, in seven pictures: buried, raised on the third day in his body, never to die again, and the firstfruits of the harvest still to come.

line.younger: The good news of Jesus in nine pictures: what went wrong between people and God, what God did about it, and the new life he gives.
line.older: The gospel in nine pictures: made for God, broken from him, and brought back by God's own act in Christ, a gift received by faith.

films.title: Grace: the gift no one earns

line.older: Grace in seven pictures: a gift and not a wage, given while we were still sinners, received with empty hands, never a licence, enough for each day, and meant to be passed on.

films.title: Faith: trusting the one who promised

line.younger: Faith is trusting God because he keeps his word. Seven pictures show what faith is, how it grows, and why even a little of it is enough.
line.older: What the Bible means by faith, in seven pictures: trust in the God who has spoken, Abraham under the stars, a father's honest prayer, faith that comes by hearing, faith that acts, and faith that walks on without seeing.

line.younger: The good news of Jesus, short enough to share, in seven pictures: what went wrong, what God did about it, and the gift he gives.
line.older: The gospel in seven pictures, short enough to share: made for God, broken from him, and brought back by God's own act in Christ, a gift received by faith.

line.older: What the church is, in seven pictures: a people, one body, living stones, a family, gathered and sent, and what churches share where they differ.

line.older: The two signs Jesus gave his church, in seven pictures: what every church shares in baptism and the Lord's Supper, and the questions on which faithful churches differ, set out without taking a side.

films.title: The Bible: how we got it

line.older: How the Bible reached us, in seven pictures: many writers over many centuries, dictation and scrolls, copying by hand, the codex, the books received as Scripture, and translation.

line.older: What prayer is, in seven pictures: talking with God as Father, the prayer Jesus taught, thanks, asking, saying sorry, waiting, and the Spirit's help when words run out.

line.older: The Christian hope in seven pictures: death named honestly, the time between death and resurrection as Christians read it, the body raised, a just judgment, and all things made new.

line.older: John 3:16 read where it was said: a night visit, a new birth, a bronze snake lifted up, the love behind the cross, and what became of the man who came in the dark.

films.title: Psalm 23: the LORD is my shepherd

line.older: Psalm 23 read line by line, as the Study Bible's notes read it: the shepherd, the right paths, the valley, the rod and the staff, the host's table, and the house at the end.

films.title: Romans 8:28: what it promises, and what it does not

line.older: One of the most quoted verses in the Bible, read in its own chapter: what it does not say, what it does, what the good is, and what the promise rests on.

line.older: A child's honest question, taken seriously in six pictures: why anything is here at all, and why the Bible says God has no beginning.

line.older: The argument from why anything exists at all, in six pictures: what it shows, what it does not, and where to weigh the case against.

line.older: Why is God unseen? Seven pictures on the family catechism's answer: God is Spirit, known in what he made, in his word, and most clearly in Jesus, with the hard objection named fairly.

line.older: Suffering is the strongest reason people give for not believing. Eight pictures on what Christians can honestly say, what they cannot, and the hope they hold.

line.younger: Can we trust a book so old, copied by hand for hundreds of years? An honest look in eight pictures.
line.older: Why would anyone trust the Bible? Eight pictures on how it was copied, what can be checked, what that proves, and what it does not.

films.title: Did Jesus really come back to life?

line.older: The historical case for the resurrection in seven pictures: the facts nearly every historian grants, the other explanations, and what history can and cannot show.

line.younger: A gentle answer to a big question, in seven pictures: what the Bible says happens when someone who belongs to Jesus dies, and why Christians can be sad and hopeful at once.
line.older: The question most people first ask beside a loss, answered plainly in seven pictures from the family catechism and the Study Bible, with the honest limits of what Christians know.

films.title: Does God still love me when I do wrong?

films.title: Are science and the Bible enemies?
